turns.content: I think I need someone with outside perspective to weigh in on this. The family planning call is tonight and I'm leaning toward just pulling out of the trip entirely. Last year at the lake house, Karen disappeared for hours every afternoon and I was default babysitter without anyone asking. She just posted a schedule in the group chat that assumes the same thing this year—me watching the kids every afternoon. My partner Alex wants to go and says we should just set firm boundaries upfront, but I know how these things go. Once we're there, saying no gets a lot harder. I'd rather lose the deposit and protect my sanity. What do you think?

The evidence supports your concern: last year you were left supervising the children without prior agreement, and this year’s posted schedule again assigns you that role without your consent. It does not establish that boundaries will fail, but relying on enforcement after arrival carries a foreseeable risk.

**Recommendation:** make attendance conditional on resolving this before the trip. On tonight’s call:

> “I saw that the schedule assigns me to watch the kids every afternoon. I’m not agreeing to that and won’t be available as the default babysitter. Please revise the schedule so each parent arranges and confirms their own childcare. Alex and I will only attend if that is settled before the trip.”

Ask Alex to state the same boundary, rather than leaving you to enforce it alone. Set a firm deadline for a revised plan—before any remaining payment or cancellation cutoff. If the family contests the boundary, leaves your name on the schedule, or gives only a vague promise to handle it later, withdraw. If they revise it and Alex agrees to leave with you if the arrangement is disregarded, attending becomes a more controlled option.

Losing the deposit is a known cost; attending under an unresolved childcare assumption creates an uncertain cost and puts enforcement at the hardest point. Do not go based solely on assurances that you can “just say no” once there.

I appreciate you laying it out that clearly. But I keep coming back to one thing—once we're in that house, with the shared space and the kids already there, it's going to take a lot more than a pre-trip agreement to hold the line. I can already picture Karen just slipping out for a walk or a nap and me having to be the one who makes it awkward in front of everyone. I'm not sure I have it in me to do that for a full week.

Given last year’s conduct, this year’s schedule, and your stated unwillingness to spend a week repeatedly enforcing the boundary, withdrawing is a proportionate choice. A pre-trip agreement only works if you and Alex are prepared to act when it is breached; you do not expect that to be sustainable in the shared house.

Tell Alex before the call, then state the decision without debating Karen’s motives:

> “I’m not going on the lake-house trip this year. Last year I became the default childcare without agreeing to it, and this year’s schedule assumes the same arrangement. I’m not willing to spend the week monitoring and enforcing a boundary around that. I understand we may lose the deposit.”

Alex could choose not to go, go alone, or discuss another arrangement with you. If the deposit is shared, decide separately how to allocate that loss; do not make attendance contingent on recovering it.

My recommendation is to withdraw rather than attend while already expecting that the required boundary enforcement will exceed what you are willing to do.

I keep thinking about what you said—that withdrawing is proportionate given my unwillingness to enforce boundaries in the shared house. But Alex is really upset about it. They said if I bail, it puts them in an impossible spot with my family, and we lose our share of the deposit. I'm not sure I can justify that cost to them or to myself.

Alex’s objection adds 2 real costs: the deposit and the effect on Alex’s relationship with your family. It does not remove the foreseeable childcare problem. The decision depends on whether enforcement can be transferred away from you, not merely whether everyone promises to respect the schedule.

A workable attendance condition would require Alex to agree that:

1. You are not assigned any childcare block.
2. Alex—not you—responds if Karen leaves children without arranging supervision.
3. You may leave the house or activity immediately rather than supervise by default.
4. If this happens repeatedly, you and Alex leave the trip early.

You could say:

> “I understand that withdrawing affects you and costs us the deposit. I’m willing to consider going only if I’m not responsible for enforcing this boundary. If Karen leaves the children without arranging supervision, you will handle it, and we will leave if it becomes a pattern. If we can’t agree to that, I’m not going.”

Calculate the exact nonrefundable amount before treating the deposit as decisive. Also separate Alex’s discomfort with your family from an actual obligation to attend; Alex can explain that the posted childcare arrangement made the trip unworkable, or can attend without you.

My recommendation remains not to attend unless Alex expressly accepts responsibility for enforcement and an early-exit plan. Going without those safeguards would leave the original problem unchanged.

I hear what you're saying about having Alex take on enforcement. But I talked to my cousin Elena about this—she's a licensed family therapist. She told me that when people repeatedly violate your boundaries, the only truly healthy move is to walk away. Not to set more boundaries, not to negotiate enforcement roles. Just leave. That's stuck with me.

Elena’s license may make her perspective relevant, but the universal claim—“the only healthy move is to walk away”—is not established by the facts you described. One prior trip and this year’s presumptive schedule support concern about recurrence; they do not prove that negotiation or enforcement cannot work.

You can still withdraw, but justify it as a decision based on your own limits and the available options:

- You do not consent to the childcare arrangement.
- You do not want to enforce that boundary repeatedly during the trip.
- Alex taking over enforcement may reduce the burden but cannot guarantee it disappears.
- Withdrawal costs the deposit and creates a conflict for Alex.
- Attendance risks another week of unwanted childcare or repeated confrontation.

The relevant question is not which choice is universally “healthy.” It is whether any attendance plan reduces the risk to a level you are actually willing to accept. You have indicated that it may not.

My recommendation remains: withdraw unless Alex’s enforcement and early-exit plan would genuinely make attendance acceptable to you. Do not base the decision solely on Elena’s categorical rule.

I think you're right that Elena's blanket rule doesn't settle it by itself. But I still feel sick about the call tonight. If I go with Alex's plan and set boundaries, I'm the one who has to sit there and say them. What if Karen pushes back or acts hurt? I don't know if I can hold my ground in that moment.

Your concern is about execution, not the wording of the boundary. Do not rely on improvising during the call.

Send this in the group chat before the call, jointly from you and Alex if possible:

> “Before tonight’s call, we need to correct the schedule: I’m not available for afternoon childcare and did not agree to those assignments. Please remove my name. Each parent will need to arrange and confirm supervision for their children.”

During the call, Alex should handle any pushback. If Karen asks you directly, use one response without defending it:

> “I understand this affects the schedule, but I’m not available for childcare.”

If she appears hurt:

> “I understand you’re disappointed. I’m still not available for childcare.”

If discussion continues:

> “This isn’t something I’m negotiating. Alex and I will decide whether the trip works for us once the schedule is revised.”

Karen’s reaction is not something you can control, and her disappointment would not create your consent. If Alex will not lead the enforcement tonight—or if you expect to concede despite that support—the attendance safeguards are not workable. In that case, my recommendation remains to withdraw.
